claim: Cr-Xbp1 is predominantly expressed in notochord and epidermis in Ciona robusta embryos.
source: We had previously identified Ciona robusta Xbp1 (Cr-Xbp1, formerly Ci-XBPa; gene model: KH.C4.516) and showed that this gene is predominantly expressed in notochord and epidermis (Figure 1A and A')
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A and A', and by previous publication (Kugler et al., 2008)

claim: Cr-Xbp1 is overexpressed in embryos ectopically expressing Ci-Bra.
source: we had also observed that Cr-Xbp1 is overexpressed in embryos ectopically expressing Ci-Bra and downregulated in transgenic embryos expressing a repressor form of Ci-Bra (Kugler et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Kugler et al., 2008)

claim: Cr-Xbp1 is downregulated in transgenic embryos expressing a repressor form of Ci-Bra.
source: we had also observed that Cr-Xbp1 is overexpressed in embryos ectopically expressing Ci-Bra and downregulated in transgenic embryos expressing a repressor form of Ci-Bra (Kugler et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Kugler et al., 2008)

claim: Embryos lacking Ci-Bra function show normal Cr-Xbp1 expression in epidermal cells and in a small region of the anterior sensory vesicle.
source: Compared to stage-matched controls hybridized in parallel (Figure 1B), embryos lacking Ci-Bra function show normal Cr-Xbp1 expression in epidermal cells and in a small region of the anterior sensory vesicle, but lack Cr-Xbp1 expression in the notochord (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by WMISH data shown in Figure 1C comparing Ci-Bra-/- mutants to wild-type controls

claim: Embryos lacking Ci-Bra function lack Cr-Xbp1 expression in the notochord.
source: Compared to stage-matched controls hybridized in parallel (Figure 1B), embryos lacking Ci-Bra function show normal Cr-Xbp1 expression in epidermal cells and in a small region of the anterior sensory vesicle, but lack Cr-Xbp1 expression in the notochord (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by WMISH data shown in Figure 1C using Ci-Bra-/- mutant embryos

claim: Ci-Bra is required for notochord expression of Cr-Xbp1.
source: To directly verify the requirement of Ci-Bra for Cr-Xbp1 notochord expression, we performed whole-mount in situ hybridization (WMISH) on embryos carrying a null mutation in the Ci-Bra coding region (Chiba et al., 2009). Compared to stage-matched controls hybridized in parallel (Figure 1B), embryos lacking Ci-Bra function show normal Cr-Xbp1 expression in epidermal cells and in a small region of the anterior sensory vesicle, but lack Cr-Xbp1 expression in the notochord (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by WMISH experiments on Ci-Bra null mutants showing loss of Cr-Xbp1 in notochord but not in other tissues

claim: Embryos electroporated with Bra>Xbp1DBD::GFP had markedly shorter tails compared to control embryos.
source: Compared to embryos electroporated with Bra>GFP (Figure 2A), embryos electroporated with Bra>Xbp1DBD::GFP had markedly shorter tails, irregularly shaped notochord cells, and displayed aberrant notochord intercalation (Figure 2B and D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images in Figure 2B showing phenotypic differences from control

claim: Embryos electroporated with Bra>Xbp1DBD::GFP had irregularly shaped notochord cells.
source: Compared to embryos electroporated with Bra>GFP (Figure 2A), embryos electroporated with Bra>Xbp1DBD::GFP had markedly shorter tails, irregularly shaped notochord cells, and displayed aberrant notochord intercalation (Figure 2B and D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images in Figure 2B and insets showing cell morphology

claim: Embryos electroporated with Bra>Xbp1DBD::GFP displayed aberrant notochord intercalation.
source: Compared to embryos electroporated with Bra>GFP (Figure 2A), embryos electroporated with Bra>Xbp1DBD::GFP had markedly shorter tails, irregularly shaped notochord cells, and displayed aberrant notochord intercalation (Figure 2B and D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Embryos expressing Xbp1 shRNA showed a phenotype milder than the one caused by Bra>Xbp1DBD::GFP, in a lower percentage of embryos.
source: In embryos expressing Xbp1 shRNA, we observed a phenotype milder than the one caused by Bra>Xbp1DBD::GFP, in a lower percentage of embryos (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 2D and images in Figure 2C

claim: Transgenic embryos carrying the Foxa.a>Xbp1FL plasmid have tails that are bent upward.
source: Transgenic embryos carrying the Foxa.a>Xbp1FL plasmid ectopically express Xbp1 in CNS and endoderm and overexpress it in the notochord. This causes the tail to be bent upward and the notochord cells to be slightly smaller than normal and often arranged into two or more rows throughout the tail (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: Supported by images in Figure 2E and F showing embryo morphology

claim: Transgenic embryos carrying the Foxa.a>Xbp1FL plasmid have notochord cells that are slightly smaller than normal and often arranged into two or more rows throughout the tail.
source: Transgenic embryos carrying the Foxa.a>Xbp1FL plasmid ectopically express Xbp1 in CNS and endoderm and overexpress it in the notochord. This causes the tail to be bent upward and the notochord cells to be slightly smaller than normal and often arranged into two or more rows throughout the tail (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: Supported by images in Figure 2E and F showing notochord cell arrangement

claim: Embryos carrying the Bra>Xbp1DBD::VP16::GFP transgene exhibited an evident change in the shape and localization of their notochord cells.
source: Compared to stage-matched control embryos (Figure 2D, G and G'), embryos carrying the Bra>Xbp1DBD::VP16::GFP transgene exhibited an evident change in the shape and localization of their notochord cells, which was dependent upon the percentage of transgene incorporation
evidence: Supported by images in Figure 2H, I, H', and I' showing notochord cell morphology and position

claim: An abnormally high number of transgenic cells was observed in the tails of embryos expressing the Xbp1DBD::VP16::GFP fusion protein.
source: we also observed an abnormally high number of transgenic cells in the tails of embryos expressing the Xbp1DBD::VP16::GFP fusion protein (Figure 2H, I, H', and I'), which might be caused either by the repositioning of mesenchymal cells from the trunk to the tail or by a loss in the control of cell division in some of the presumptive notochord cells.
evidence: Supported by images in Figure 2H, I, H', and I' showing increased cell numbers

claim: The abnormally high number of transgenic cells in Xbp1DBD::VP16::GFP embryos might be caused by the repositioning of mesenchymal cells from the trunk to the tail.
source: we also observed an abnormally high number of transgenic cells in the tails of embryos expressing the Xbp1DBD::VP16::GFP fusion protein (Figure 2H, I, H', and I'), which might be caused either by the repositioning of mesenchymal cells from the trunk to the tail or by a loss in the control of cell division in some of the presumptive notochord cells.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed phenotype

claim: The abnormally high number of transgenic cells in Xbp1DBD::VP16::GFP embryos might be caused by a loss in the control of cell division in some of the presumptive notochord cells.
source: we also observed an abnormally high number of transgenic cells in the tails of embryos expressing the Xbp1DBD::VP16::GFP fusion protein (Figure 2H, I, H', and I'), which might be caused either by the repositioning of mesenchymal cells from the trunk to the tail or by a loss in the control of cell division in some of the presumptive notochord cells.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed phenotype

claim: 109 individual putative target genes of Cr-Xbp1 were identified through microarray screens.
source: After these microarray screens were carried out in triplicate, 109 individual putative target genes of Cr-Xbp1 were identified.
evidence: Supported by microarray experiments performed in triplicate

claim: 71 of the 100 expression patterns analyzed include notochord cells, their precursors, and/or broader territories encompassing the notochord.
source: In total, 71 of the 100 expression patterns (71%) include notochord cells, their precursors, and/or broader territories encompassing the notochord (Supplementary file 1, Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3 and supplementary figures

claim: The expression of Cr-Xbp1-downstream genes in trunk endoderm and mesenchyme reflects the late expression of Cr-Xbp1 reported in these tissues at the larva stage.
source: The expression of Cr-Xbp1-downstream genes in trunk endoderm and mesenchyme reflects the late expression of Cr-Xbp1 reported in these tissues at the larva stage (Kusakabe et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Kusakabe et al., 2002)

claim: Morpholino-mediated inactivation of KH.C12.323, which encodes for an aquaporin channel, causes the disorganization of the body plan.
source: According to previous functional studies, morpholino-mediated inactivation of one of the genes downstream of Cr-Xbp1, KH.C12.323, which encodes for an aquaporin channel, causes the disorganization of the body plan (KH.C12.323, cicl027n09; Hamada et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous functional study (Hamada et al., 2007)

claim: The Cr-Xbp1 target genes expressed in epidermis include Pitx.
source: The Cr-Xbp1 target genes expressed in epidermis include Pitx, a well-characterized homeobox gene mainly expressed in the anterior sensory vesicle, epidermis, and oral siphon primordium (Christiaen et al., 2002; Christiaen et al., 2005), and Nodal, the activator responsible for Pitx asymmetric expression in the epidermis of the left side of the embryo (Yoshida and Saiga, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous characterizations of Pitx (Christiaen et al., 2002; Christiaen et al., 2005)

claim: The Cr-Xbp1 target genes expressed in epidermis include Nodal.
source: The Cr-Xbp1 target genes expressed in epidermis include Pitx, a well-characterized homeobox gene mainly expressed in the anterior sensory vesicle, epidermis, and oral siphon primordium (Christiaen et al., 2002; Christiaen et al., 2005), and Nodal, the activator responsible for Pitx asymmetric expression in the epidermis of the left side of the embryo (Yoshida and Saiga, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Yoshida and Saiga, 2008)

claim: Nodal is the activator responsible for Pitx asymmetric expression in the epidermis of the left side of the embryo.
source: The Cr-Xbp1 target genes expressed in epidermis include Pitx, a well-characterized homeobox gene mainly expressed in the anterior sensory vesicle, epidermis, and oral siphon primordium (Christiaen et al., 2002; Christiaen et al., 2005), and Nodal, the activator responsible for Pitx asymmetric expression in the epidermis of the left side of the embryo (Yoshida and Saiga, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Yoshida and Saiga, 2008)

claim: Cr-Xbp1 is expressed in the epidermis of both trunk and tail.
source: These findings are consistent with the expression of Cr-Xbp1 in the epidermis of both trunk and tail (Figure 1A and A') and in the anterior sensory vesicle (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A and A'

claim: Cr-Xbp1 is expressed in the anterior sensory vesicle.
source: These findings are consistent with the expression of Cr-Xbp1 in the epidermis of both trunk and tail (Figure 1A and A') and in the anterior sensory vesicle (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1B and C

claim: Cr-Xbp1 is expressed after metamorphosis in the newly formed endostyle.
source: In addition to being expressed during embryogenesis, Cr-Xbp1 is also detected after metamorphosis, in the newly formed endostyle, a structure homologous to the vertebrate thyroid gland (e.g., Sasaki et al., 2003), in circulating hemocytes, and in part of the digestive tract (Ogasawara et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Sasaki et al., 2003; Ogasawara et al., 2002)

claim: The endostyle is a structure homologous to the vertebrate thyroid gland.
source: In addition to being expressed during embryogenesis, Cr-Xbp1 is also detected after metamorphosis, in the newly formed endostyle, a structure homologous to the vertebrate thyroid gland (e.g., Sasaki et al., 2003), in circulating hemocytes, and in part of the digestive tract (Ogasawara et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Sasaki et al., 2003)

claim: Cr-Xbp1 is expressed in circulating hemocytes after metamorphosis.
source: In addition to being expressed during embryogenesis, Cr-Xbp1 is also detected after metamorphosis, in the newly formed endostyle, a structure homologous to the vertebrate thyroid gland (e.g., Sasaki et al., 2003), in circulating hemocytes, and in part of the digestive tract (Ogasawara et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Ogasawara et al., 2002)

claim: Cr-Xbp1 is expressed in part of the digestive tract after metamorphosis.
source: In addition to being expressed during embryogenesis, Cr-Xbp1 is also detected after metamorphosis, in the newly formed endostyle, a structure homologous to the vertebrate thyroid gland (e.g., Sasaki et al., 2003), in circulating hemocytes, and in part of the digestive tract (Ogasawara et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Ogasawara et al., 2002)

claim: No overlap was found between the notochord genes downstream of Cr-Xbp1 and those controlled by Bhlh-tun1.
source: No overlap was found between the notochord genes downstream of Cr-Xbp1 and those controlled by another node of the Ciona notochord GRN, the ascidian-specific transcription factor Bhlh-tun1 (Kugler et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by comparison with previous work (Kugler et al., 2019)

claim: In control Ciona embryos carrying the Bra>GFP transgene, Ci-Bra mRNA is detected in all 40 notochord cells.
source: In control Ciona embryos carrying the developmentally neutral Bra>GFP transgene, the notochord develops normally and Ci-Bra mRNA is detected in all of its 40 cells (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: Supported by fluorescent in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4A-C

claim: At the mid-tailbud stage, the notochord cells are columnar in shape and exhibit a 'stack of coins' arrangement.
source: At the mid-tailbud stage, the notochord cells are columnar in shape and exhibit a 'stack of coins' arrangement (Figure 4C, Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images in Figure 4C

claim: In embryos carrying the Bra>Xbp1DBD::GFP construct, the notochord is mostly composed of irregularly shaped cells.
source: In embryos carrying the Bra>Xbp1DBD::GFP construct (Figure 4D–F), the notochord is mostly composed of irregularly shaped cells, and only the cells that have not received this transgene express Ci-Bra (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images in Figure 4D-F

claim: In embryos carrying the Bra>Xbp1DBD::GFP construct, only the cells that have not received this transgene express Ci-Bra.
source: In embryos carrying the Bra>Xbp1DBD::GFP construct (Figure 4D–F), the notochord is mostly composed of irregularly shaped cells, and only the cells that have not received this transgene express Ci-Bra (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by fluorescent in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4E

claim: The repressor form of Cr-Xbp1 is able to repress Ci-Bra expression.
source: The lack of overlap between the cells carrying the Bra>Xbp1DBD::GFP construct (Figure 4D) and the cells expressing Ci-Bra (Figure 4E) indicates that the repressor form of Cr-Xbp1 is able to repress Ci-Bra expression (Figure 4F, Figure 4—video 2).
evidence: Supported by fluorescent in situ hybridization data showing lack of overlap between transgene and Ci-Bra expression in Figure 4D-F

claim: Fibrillin is uniformly expressed in the notochord in control embryos.
source: As predicted by the results of the microarray screens (Supplementary file 1), fibrillin is uniformly expressed in the notochord in control embryos (Figure 4G), while in Bra>Xbp1DBD::VP16::GFP transgenic embryos expression of this gene is limited to the notochord cells that did not incorporate the transgene (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4G

claim: In Bra>Xbp1DBD::VP16::GFP transgenic embryos, expression of fibrillin is limited to the notochord cells that did not incorporate the transgene.
source: As predicted by the results of the microarray screens (Supplementary file 1), fibrillin is uniformly expressed in the notochord in control embryos (Figure 4G), while in Bra>Xbp1DBD::VP16::GFP transgenic embryos expression of this gene is limited to the notochord cells that did not incorporate the transgene (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4H

claim: The repressive activity of the Xbp1DBD::VP16 fusion on fibrillin is likely indirect and could be due to the activation of a repressor of fibrillin expression.
source: This repressive activity of the Xbp1DBD::VP16 fusion is likely indirect and could be due to the activation of a repressor of fibrillin expression; alternatively, the Xbp1DBD::VP16 transgene might be solely occupying the Xbp1 binding sites in the regulatory regions of this and other Cr-Xbp1-downstream genes without being able to activate their expression, thus preventing the endogenous Cr-Xbp1 and/or other activators from binding.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed repression

claim: The Xbp1DBD::VP16 transgene might be solely occupying the Xbp1 binding sites in the regulatory regions of Cr-Xbp1-downstream genes without being able to activate their expression.
source: This repressive activity of the Xbp1DBD::VP16 fusion is likely indirect and could be due to the activation of a repressor of fibrillin expression; alternatively, the Xbp1DBD::VP16 transgene might be solely occupying the Xbp1 binding sites in the regulatory regions of this and other Cr-Xbp1-downstream genes without being able to activate their expression, thus preventing the endogenous Cr-Xbp1 and/or other activators from binding.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for the observed repression

claim: Xbra/Tbxt is expressed throughout the mesoderm during gastrulation in Xenopus.
source: In Xenopus, Xbra/Tbxt is expressed throughout the mesoderm during gastrulation and in the prospective notochord at neurula stages (Smith et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Smith et al., 1991)

claim: Xbra/Tbxt is expressed in the prospective notochord at neurula stages in Xenopus.
source: In Xenopus, Xbra/Tbxt is expressed throughout the mesoderm during gastrulation and in the prospective notochord at neurula stages (Smith et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Smith et al., 1991)

claim: Xbp1 is first detected in the dorsal lip of the blastopore at the early gastrula stage in Xenopus.
source: Xbp1 is first detected in the dorsal lip of the blastopore at the early gastrula stage and persists in the involuting dorsal mesoderm as gastrulation proceeds (Zhao et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Zhao et al., 2003)

claim: Xbp1 persists in the involuting dorsal mesoderm as gastrulation proceeds in Xenopus.
source: Xbp1 is first detected in the dorsal lip of the blastopore at the early gastrula stage and persists in the involuting dorsal mesoderm as gastrulation proceeds (Zhao et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Zhao et al., 2003)

claim: Nearly all Xbra morphant embryos showed reduced Xbp1 expression at the gastrula stage compared to their stage-matched controls.
source: We found that nearly all Xbra morphant embryos showed reduced Xbp1 expression at the gastrula stage compared to their stage-matched controls (Figure 5A, B, B' and G).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5A, B, B' and quantification in Figure 5G

claim: Approximately 65% of the Xbp1 morphant embryos displayed reduced Xbra expression at gastrula stages.
source: Our results show that Xbp1 is implicated in the regulation of Xbra expression in the dorsal mesoderm, as approximately 65% of the Xbp1 morphant embryos displayed reduced Xbra expression at gastrula stages (Figure 5C, D, D' and H).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5C, D, D' and quantification in Figure 5H

claim: Xbp1 is implicated in the regulation of Xbra expression in the dorsal mesoderm.
source: Our results show that Xbp1 is implicated in the regulation of Xbra expression in the dorsal mesoderm, as approximately 65% of the Xbp1 morphant embryos displayed reduced Xbra expression at gastrula stages (Figure 5C, D, D' and H).
evidence: Supported by morpholino knockdown experiments showing reduced Xbra expression in Xbp1 morphants

claim: The phenotype of XbraMOS-injected embryos was identical to the phenotype generated by the injection of the Xbra translation-blocking MO.
source: The phenotype of XbraMOS- (Figure 5E, E' and G) and Xbp1MOS-injected embryos (Figure 5F, F' and H) was identical to the phenotype generated by the injection of their respective translation-blocking MO.
evidence: Supported by comparison of phenotypes shown in Figure 5 panels E, E', G and quantification

claim: The phenotype of Xbp1MOS-injected embryos was identical to the phenotype generated by the injection of the Xbp1 translation-blocking MO.
source: The phenotype of XbraMOS- (Figure 5E, E' and G) and Xbp1MOS-injected embryos (Figure 5F, F' and H) was identical to the phenotype generated by the injection of their respective translation-blocking MO.
evidence: Supported by comparison of phenotypes shown in Figure 5 panels F, F', H and quantification

claim: Xbra and Xbp1 morphant embryos displayed axis elongation defects.
source: Later in development, unlike stage-matched controls (Figure 6), Xbra and Xbp1 morphant embryos displayed axis elongation defects (Figure 6B and C) and posterior truncations (Figure 6B' and C').
evidence: Supported by images of morphant embryos in Figure 6B and C

claim: Xbra and Xbp1 morphant embryos displayed posterior truncations.
source: Later in development, unlike stage-matched controls (Figure 6), Xbra and Xbp1 morphant embryos displayed axis elongation defects (Figure 6B and C) and posterior truncations (Figure 6B' and C').
evidence: Supported by images of morphant embryos in Figure 6B' and C'

claim: The malformations in Xbra and Xbp1 morphant embryos are similar to those observed upon expression of a dominant-interfering Xbra::Engrailed fusion.
source: Overall, these malformations are similar to those observed upon expression of a dominant-interfering Xbra::Engrailed fusion in previous studies (Xbra-EnR; Conlon et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by comparison with previous work (Conlon et al., 1996)

claim: Shh expression is discontinuous in the notochord of Xbra and Xbp1 morphant embryos.
source: WMISH of Xenopus embryos at NF stage 35/36 with a Shh probe indicates that, compared to sibling controls, Shh expression is discontinuous in the notochord of Xbra and Xbp1 morphant embryos, and often confined to its posterior regions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Shh expression is often confined to posterior regions of the notochord in Xbra and Xbp1 morphant embryos.
source: WMISH of Xenopus embryos at NF stage 35/36 with a Shh probe indicates that, compared to sibling controls, Shh expression is discontinuous in the notochord of Xbra and Xbp1 morphant embryos, and often confined to its posterior regions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Notochord differentiation is impaired by alterations in the Xbra-Xbp1 subcircuit.
source: These results suggest that notochord differentiation is impaired by alterations in the Xbra-Xbp1 subcircuit.
evidence: This is inferred from the discontinuous Shh expression in morphant embryos

claim: Xbp1 and Xbra regulate each other's expression as part of a regulatory loop controlling formation of dorsal mesoderm.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that Xbp1 and Xbra regulate each other's expression as part of a regulatory loop controlling not only formation of dorsal mesoderm, but also notochord development and differentiation.
evidence: This is inferred from the reciprocal regulation experiments in Xenopus

claim: Xbp1 and Xbra regulate each other's expression as part of a regulatory loop controlling notochord development and differentiation.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that Xbp1 and Xbra regulate each other's expression as part of a regulatory loop controlling not only formation of dorsal mesoderm, but also notochord development and differentiation.
evidence: This is inferred from the reciprocal regulation experiments in Xenopus

claim: The transcription factors Brachyury and Foxa2 are indispensable for notochord development.
source: Studies in organisms representative of all chordate subdivisions have provided evidence that the transcription factors Brachyury and Foxa2 are indispensable for notochord development and constitute an evolutionarily conserved subcircuit of the gene regulatory network (GRN) underlying this process (Stott et al., 1993; Ang and Rossant, 1994; Passamaneck et al., 2009; Tamplin et al., 2011; Di Gregorio, 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work across different organisms (Stott et al., 1993; Ang and Rossant, 1994; Passamaneck et al., 2009; Tamplin et al., 2011; Di Gregorio, 2020)

claim: Brachyury and Foxa2 constitute an evolutionarily conserved subcircuit of the gene regulatory network underlying notochord development.
source: Studies in organisms representative of all chordate subdivisions have provided evidence that the transcription factors Brachyury and Foxa2 are indispensable for notochord development and constitute an evolutionarily conserved subcircuit of the gene regulatory network (GRN) underlying this process (Stott et al., 1993; Ang and Rossant, 1994; Passamaneck et al., 2009; Tamplin et al., 2011; Di Gregorio, 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work (Stott et al., 1993; Ang and Rossant, 1994; Passamaneck et al., 2009; Tamplin et al., 2011; Di Gregorio, 2020)

claim: The Ciona notochord develops within approximately 1 day after fertilization.
source: The Ciona notochord develops within approximately 1 day after fertilization (Hotta et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Hotta et al., 2007)

claim: During notochord development, the high secretory activity of the notochord cells gives rise to the formation of the notochordal sheath.
source: during this time, the high secretory activity of the notochord cells gives rise to the formation of the notochordal sheath, while a fluid-filled lumen forms in the center of the notochord (Denker, 2012; Dong et al., 2009; Deng et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Denker, 2012; Dong et al., 2009; Deng et al., 2013)

claim: A fluid-filled lumen forms in the center of the notochord during development.
source: during this time, the high secretory activity of the notochord cells gives rise to the formation of the notochordal sheath, while a fluid-filled lumen forms in the center of the notochord (Denker, 2012; Dong et al., 2009; Deng et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Denker, 2012; Dong et al., 2009; Deng et al., 2013)

claim: The pressure exerted on the rigid notochordal sheath by the lumen provides the tail with a hydrostatic skeleton.
source: The pressure exerted on the rigid notochordal sheath by the lumen provides the tail with a hydrostatic skeleton along which rest the muscle cells flanking the notochord, whose contractions enable the larvae to swim (Bone, 1992; Kier, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Bone, 1992; Kier, 2012)

claim: Xbp1 is a basic leucine-zipper transcription factor that regulates the unfolded protein response.
source: Among them is the Ciona counterpart of X-box binding protein 1 (Xbp1) (Kugler et al., 2008), a basic leucine-zipper transcription factor that regulates the unfolded protein response (UPR) (Mai and Breeden, 1997; Yoshida et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Mai and Breeden, 1997; Yoshida et al., 2001)

claim: The UPR of the endoplasmic reticulum is an evolutionarily conserved mechanism that allows cells to counteract the stress caused by the presence of improperly folded proteins in the ER.
source: The UPR of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is an evolutionarily conserved mechanism that allows cells to counteract the stress caused by the presence of improperly folded proteins in the ER (Yap et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Yap et al., 2021)

claim: Three ER-stress sensors, Ire1, Perk, and Atf6, are responsible for the activation of the transcription factors Xbp1, Atf4, and Atf6-alpha, respectively, in metazoans.
source: Three ER-stress sensors, Ire1, Perk, and Atf6, are responsible, in metazoans, for the activation of the transcription factors Xbp1, Atf4, and Atf6-alpha, respectively (Hollien, 2013; Mitra and Ryoo, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Hollien, 2013; Mitra and Ryoo, 2019)

claim: Xbp1, Atf4, and Atf6-alpha regulate the expression of genes whose products decrease global protein synthesis and enhance the ability of the ER to fold proteins.
source: In turn, these transcription factors regulate the expression of genes whose products decrease global protein synthesis and enhance the ability of the ER to fold proteins, ultimately restoring proteostasis (Walter and Ron, 2011; Han and Kaufman, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Walter and Ron, 2011; Han and Kaufman, 2017)

claim: Physiological processes that challenge the ER, such as an elevated secretory activity, can activate the UPR.
source: Physiological processes that challenge the ER, such as an elevated secretory activity, can also activate the UPR; this explains the widespread role of Xbp1 in the development of plasma cells and other cells with sustained secretory activity (Reimold et al., 2001; Iwakoshi et al., 2003; Shaffer et al., 2004; Tanegashima et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Reimold et al., 2001; Iwakoshi et al., 2003; Shaffer et al., 2004; Tanegashima et al., 2009)

claim: Loss of Xbp1 in Drosophila is embryonic lethal.
source: Loss of Xbp1 in Drosophila is embryonic lethal (Souid et al., 2007), and Xbp1-knockout mice develop hypoplastic livers and die in utero from anemia (Reimold et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Souid et al., 2007)

claim: Xbp1-knockout mice develop hypoplastic livers and die in utero from anemia.
source: Loss of Xbp1 in Drosophila is embryonic lethal (Souid et al., 2007), and Xbp1-knockout mice develop hypoplastic livers and die in utero from anemia (Reimold et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Reimold et al., 2000)

claim: Xenopus Xbp1 regulates expression of the chaperone proteins Hsp5A/Bip, DNAJ9B, and HSP90B1.
source: Xenopus Xbp1 regulates expression of the chaperone proteins Hsp5A/Bip, DNAJ9B, and HSP90B1 (Tanegashima et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Tanegashima et al., 2009)

claim: Xenopus Xbp1 forms a regulatory loop with BMP-4 in the control of mesoderm and neural differentiation.
source: Xenopus Xbp1 regulates expression of the chaperone proteins Hsp5A/Bip, DNAJ9B, and HSP90B1 (Tanegashima et al., 2009), forms a regulatory loop with BMP-4 in the control of mesoderm and neural differentiation (Zhao et al., 2003; Cao et al., 2006), and is required for pancreas development (Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Zhao et al., 2003; Cao et al., 2006)

claim: Xenopus Xbp1 is required for pancreas development.

evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Yang et al., 2020)

claim: The regulation of BMP-4 by Xbp1 is present in the Ciona notochord.

evidence: Supported by the microarray data identifying BMP-4 as a Cr-Xbp1 target

claim: DnaJc7 is a notochord target of Cr-Xbp1.

claim: The regulatory connection between Brachyury and Xbp1 is maintained in Xenopus.

claim: A ChIP-on-chip study on mouse cells has uncovered 545 transcriptional targets of XBP1.

claim: At least half of the Cr-Xbp1-downstream genes with traceable vertebrate orthologs can be predicted to be participating in the UPR.

evidence: This is inferred from comparison of gene ontologies with known XBP1 targets

claim: Xbp1 is expressed in osteoblasts and chondroblasts of several skeletal structures in mouse embryos.

claim: The Xbp1-/- mutation is embryonic lethal beginning at day E12.5 in mice.

claim: Xbp1 mutant mice might have defects in notochord formation.

claim: Xbp1 is expressed in the chick notochord.

evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Bell et al., 2004; Darnell et al., 2007)

claim: Xbp1 and UPR genes have been incorporated into notochord formation early during chordate evolution.

evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of Xbp1 expression and function in notochord across chordates

evidence: Supported by the reciprocal regulation experiments in both Ciona and Xenopus

claim: 36 of the 71 Cr-Xbp1-downstream notochord genes had been previously reported as targets of Ci-Bra.

claim: Genes that mediate UPR are activated under physiological conditions in cells specialized in secretion.
source: In addition to participating in the response to ER stress, genes that mediate UPR are also activated under physiological conditions in cells specialized in secretion, such as hepatocytes (Reimold et al., 2000), plasma cells (Iwakoshi et al., 2003), pancreatic acinar cells (Lee et al., 2005), cells of the salivary glands (Lee et al., 2005), cells of the hatching gland in fish (Bennett et al., 2007), and the notochord cells of zebrafish and Xenopus (Bennett et al., 2007; Tanegashima et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work (Reimold et al., 2000; Iwakoshi et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2005; Bennett et al., 2007; Tanegashima et al., 2009)

claim: Cr-Xbp1 controls evolutionarily conserved UPR effectors, such as proteases, chaperones, and other mediators of intracellular trafficking and protein recycling.
source: We have determined that Cr-Xbp1 controls evolutionarily conserved UPR effectors, such as proteases, chaperones, and other mediators of intracellular trafficking and protein recycling, including Vps35l and Clvs1 (Singla et al., 2019; Katoh et al., 2009), and the serine/threonine-protein kinase Dapk1, which acts as a UPR sensor and as a mediator of apoptosis and autophagy (Singh et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by the microarray data and citations to previous work (Singla et al., 2019; Katoh et al., 2009; Singh et al., 2016)

claim: Autophagy allows cells to selectively degrade misfolded proteins and defective organelles in response to stress signals.

claim: The regulation of olfactomedin 2 by Cr-Xbp1 is likely indirect.
